phase1.intro:
Every program I've shown you so far just runs and prints — but real programs usually need to actually listen to the person using them.

Want to start with how Scanner reads input, or the gotcha that catches everyone?

topics.buttonText: How do I actually read input from the user?
dialogue: That's what [[term:Scanner]] is for. First you import it — `import java.util.Scanner;` — then build one wired to the console: `Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);`.
Once that's built, `.nextLine()` reads a whole line of text, `.nextInt()` reads a whole number, and `.nextDouble()` reads a decimal.

stickyNote.definition: java.util.Scanner reads console input. new Scanner(System.in) creates one; .nextLine(), .nextInt(), .nextDouble() read different types.

topics.buttonText: What's the gotcha everyone falls into?
dialogue: [[warn:Here's the gotcha that gets literally everyone at least once]]: `.nextInt()` reads the number, but leaves the leftover newline character sitting in the buffer.

If you call `.nextLine()` right after `.nextInt()`, it immediately grabs that leftover newline and hands you back an empty string instead of waiting for real input. [[key:The fix is an extra scanner.nextLine() right after nextInt()]] to clear that leftover newline first.

stickyNote.flavor: 🕳️ the leftover newline everyone falls into once
stickyNote.definition: nextInt() leaves a trailing newline in the buffer. A nextLine() called right after grabs that newline instead of new input — fix with an extra nextLine() to clear it.

topics.buttonText: Do I need to clean anything up after?
dialogue: Don't forget `scanner.close()` when you're done — it's just good manners, releasing the resource back once you're finished listening.

stickyNote.flavor: 🚪 politely hanging up when you're done listening
stickyNote.definition: Releases the Scanner's underlying resource once input reading is finished. Call it after your last read.

phase2.errorMessage:
Enter your age: 25
Enter your name: Name: , Age: 25

(No error message — but the program SKIPS the name input!)
phase2.explanation:
Nothing crashed here — which is honestly worse, because [[warn:silent bugs are harder to catch than loud ones]]. After `scanner.nextInt()` reads the age, a leftover newline character is still sitting in the input buffer. The very next `scanner.nextLine()` doesn't wait for you to type anything — it immediately reads that leftover newline and hands back an empty string.

[[key:The fix is one extra line]]: call `scanner.nextLine()` right after `scanner.nextInt()`, just to clear that leftover newline, before you call `scanner.nextLine()` again for the actual input you want.

phase3.openingDialogue: Now let's make your program actually TALK to the user~ 💬

mcq.question:
Why does calling scanner.nextLine() right after scanner.nextInt() sometimes return an empty string?

A) nextInt() closes the Scanner
B) nextInt() leaves a leftover newline in the input buffer that nextLine() reads immediately
C) nextLine() only works before nextInt()
D) Scanner can only be used once per program

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Asks for a user's favorite color (String)
2. Asks for their lucky number (int)
3. Prints: "Your favorite color is [color] and your lucky number is [number]"

Handle the nextInt buffer issue correctly!

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: Scanner wasn't Java's original way to read console input — it was added in Java 5 (2004) as a friendlier wrapper. Under the hood it actually uses regular expressions to figure out where one token ends and the next begins, which is part of why it's a bit slower than lower-level input methods, though you'd never notice it at a beginner's scale.
phase5.openingDialogue: Before you go talk to your program some more~
